title: The tyranny of school metrics
author: Hart, Nick
summary: Nick Hart applies Jerry Muller's 'tyranny of metrics' thesis to schools, arguing that the obsession with measurable proxies for learning has displaced the professional judgment and expertise that actually produce good education. Hart shows how school metrics — attendance rates, Progress 8 scores, exam results — come to substitute for the complex reality they were designed to illuminate, producing Goodhart's Law dynamics that corrupt the very things being measured. He traces how school leaders respond to accountability pressure in ways that are individually rational but systemically destructive, and shows this pattern is structural rather than personal. The article distinguishes between the legitimate use of data as one input among many and the delegitimisation of teacher judgment that occurs when metrics become the primary language of school quality. Hart concludes that schools need leaders who can hold the tension between accountability demands and the irreducible complexity of human development.
points: Jerry Muller's tyranny of metrics maps directly onto schools: measurable proxies for learning come to replace the learning itself.
When metrics become targets they are no longer good measures — Goodhart's Law is endemic in school accountability systems and its effects are cumulative.
School leaders respond rationally to accountability pressure in ways that harm students, because the incentive is the metric rather than the actual outcome.
Professional judgment — the irreducible expertise of teachers and leaders who know their students — is systematically delegitimised when metrics dominate institutional language.
Schools need leaders who can hold the tension between accountability demands and the irreducible complexity of human development without collapsing one into the other.
quotes: Trust is such a complex concept that leaders would have to have to prepare a combination of very carefully planned questions, along with additional methods of gathering information such as observing interactions, all underpinned by a sound understanding of what it is that actually contributes to high levels of relational trust.

Bryk and Sneider identified four attributes needed to build trusting relationships: It would be difficult to write survey questions that yield responses that get to the root of why levels of relational trust are what they are and so a more fluid conversation might be a better way of evaluating a desired outcome such as this.

The Headteacher, naturally, knows exactly what those areas for improvement are and, regarding the one that referenced a need to improve behaviour (particularly around low level disruption), responds by telling their interviewer that senior staff have attended behaviour training provided by the local authority.

As in the first example, the Headteacher has given no consideration to how well staff have implemented any strategies developed as a result of the work with the local authority’s behaviour adviser or indeed whether behaviour is actually any better than it was at the time of the previous inspection.

Such evaluation relies on the knowledge of the person doing it – if they do not fully understand how relational trust is built and maintained, they will not be able to effectively find out information related to it, hence the importance of building leaders’ knowledge of evaluation mechanisms.

The vicious circle between metrics and trust There is a reasonable assumption to be made that school leaders who deliberately plan for the difference that they aim to make and evaluate the extent to which it has been achieved will stand a good chance of bringing about school improvement.

Here’s another example: A Headteacher is sitting across the table from governors, their MAT line manager or an HMI and is asked what progress the school has made towards the areas for improvement published in the most recent Ofsted report from last year’s inspection.
